tour.title: Centro & Lapa: Colonial Streets & the Selarón Steps
tour.summary: An empire that landed at the water, a belle-époque opera house, an 1894 tearoom and a Chilean artist's tiled staircase — a short, flat weekday walk through old downtown to Lapa.
tour.overviewText:
Rio de Janeiro is the city the world thinks it knows — beaches, carnival, a giant Christ with his arms out. This walk goes to the part that made all of it possible and that most visitors never see: the Centro, the old downtown, where Brazil was invented. For nearly two centuries Rio was the capital of Brazil, and for thirteen years it was the capital of the entire Portuguese empire — the only European empire ever ruled from outside Europe. The streets you are about to walk held the court, the treasury, the opera house and the newspaper that told the country what to think.

The story turns on 1808, when Napoleon's army marched on Lisbon and the Portuguese royal family fled across the Atlantic — not a few courtiers but roughly ten thousand people, escorted by the British navy, arriving in a colonial town with no palace fit for a king. Rio improvised, and in improvising became something new: the seat of an empire and then, after Prince Pedro declared independence in 1822, the capital of the Empire of Brazil. That is why this district looks the way it does. The colonial square by the water, the church the exiled king attended, the Parisian opera house built a century later to prove the young republic was civilised — each is a layer of the same argument about what Brazil should be.

Today the Centro is the city's financial heart and, after dark and on weekends, an almost empty one. Banks, oil companies and the state oil giant Petrobras fill its towers by day; commuters drain out by evening; the streets that were crowded at noon are quiet and more exposed at night. That emptiness is the reason to walk it on a weekday, in daylight, finishing in Lapa as the bars open — and the reason this tour is honest about pickpockets on the main avenues rather than pretending the romance cancels the risk. Lapa itself, the old bohemian quarter at the end, is the exception: samba clubs and nineteenth-century mansions, alive from late afternoon.

The walk is short and mostly flat — about five kilometres and roughly seventy-five minutes of walking, four to five hours if you linger at every stop. It begins at the water at Praça XV, moves south through the old civic and religious core, stops for coffee in a belle-époque tearoom, then loops west to climb the tiled staircase a Chilean artist spent twenty-three years covering, and ends beneath the colonial aqueduct arches where Lapa's nightlife starts. Nothing is strenuous except those steps, and you can take them slowly or skip them. Everything is on the metro — Cinelândia and Carioca stations are steps from the route — and the metro fare is R$7.90 (verify at the gate). Prices in this tour are in reais, the Brazilian currency; R$1 is one hundred centavos.

Come on a weekday, start after breakfast, wear shoes that grip cobblestones, keep your phone in a front pocket on the crowded stretches, and finish with a caipirinha under the arches. This is the Rio that was a capital before it was a postcard.
tour.difficulty: Easy, mostly flat, on city pavements and cobblestones. One real climb: the 215 tiled steps of the Escadaria Selarón, steep and uneven, which you can take slowly or skip. Long stretches in the sun with little shade.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: A weekday, starting mid-morning around 10:00 so the churches and the tearoom are open, finishing in Lapa in the late afternoon as the bars open. Avoid weekends, when the Centro empties and feels more exposed, and avoid the historic centre after dark except for Lapa's main streets.

stops.name: Praça XV & the Paço Imperial
stops.narration:
Stand with your back to the water. This square, Praça XV — short for Praça Quinze de Novembro, the Fifteenth of November Square, named for the date in 1889 when Brazil's monarchy was overthrown — was the front door of an empire, and the low stone building on its far side is the reason. 'Paço' means palace; this one began in 1743 as the house and office of the colonial governor, designed by the military engineer José Fernandes Pinto Alpoim. When the colony's capital moved from Salvador to Rio in 1763, it became the Viceroy's Palace. Then, in 1808, everything changed.

Napoleon's army was marching on Lisbon, and the Portuguese royal family did something no European monarchy had done: it fled across the ocean. Roughly ten thousand people — Queen Maria I, her son Prince Regent João, the court, the treasury, the archives — crossed the Atlantic under British escort and landed here. Rio had no building fit for a king, so this one was promoted: the Royal Palace, seat of the entire Portuguese empire, which for thirteen years was governed from South America. Historians call it a metropolitan reversal — the colony ruling the empire. Courtiers kissed the king's hand in a throne room upstairs in a ceremony called the beija-mão, the hand-kiss, and the city filled with nobles who had arrived with little and now needed houses, so ordinary families were evicted to make room.

Brazil's independence was declared from this square's orbit. On 9 January 1822, João's son Pedro refused Portugal's order to return home — the Dia do Fico, the 'I stay' day — and in September that year he proclaimed an independent empire with himself as emperor. The palace became the Paço Imperial, the emperors' office rather than their home, and from it Brazil was ruled until 1889. In 1888, in a room here, Pedro II's daughter Princess Isabel, acting as regent, signed the Lei Áurea — the Golden Law — which abolished slavery in Brazil, the last country in the Americas to do so.

Walk around the square: the old cathedral across it was the royal chapel, linked to the palace by an elevated passageway so the court could cross unseen. Ferries leave from the far end for Niterói, the city across Guanabara Bay. The palace is free to enter as a cultural centre, with exhibitions; it typically opens Tuesday to Sunday, so verify at the door. Stay on the busy side, and do not linger here after dark — the waterfront empties fast.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The square is free. The Paço Imperial is free to enter as a cultural centre; special exhibitions occasionally charge. Verify hours at the door.
stops.openingHours: Praça XV is open at all hours. The Paço Imperial cultural centre is typically open Tuesday to Sunday, roughly midday into the late afternoon; confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Flat cobbled square, step-free along the waterfront. The Paço has a few steps at the entrance and level galleries inside.
stops.insiderTip: Find the marble fountain, the Fonte de Mestre Valentim, at the water end of the square, and look for the elevated passageway at the back of the palace that once let the court cross to the old cathedral unseen.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the square at its southern end and walk about five hundred metres down Rua Primeiro de Março, the old colonial high street, then bear left toward the twin towers of the Candelária Church on Praça Pio X. It is straight and level, busy with office workers on weekdays.

stops.name: Candelária Church
stops.narration:
The two towers ahead belong to the Igreja da Candelária, the Church of Our Lady of Candelária — Candlemas, the feast of the Presentation of Jesus, on 2 February. The legend is a shipwreck. A vessel called the Candelária nearly went down in a storm, and a Portuguese couple aboard swore to build a chapel if they survived; the chapel they sponsored went up around 1609. The present church is far bigger. Work began in 1775 to a design by the military engineer Francisco João Roscio, and it was inaugurated — still unfinished — in 1811, with King João VI in the congregation, which tells you how quickly this church became the empire's church. The façade is Portuguese colonial Baroque; the inside was redone later in Neo-Renaissance marble; the dome, finished in 1877, was carved from pale Lioz stone in Lisbon and shipped across the Atlantic, and when it went up it was the tallest thing in Rio.

Inside, enslaved people were baptised, among them Rosa Egipcíaca, the first Black woman known to have written a book in Brazil — a volume of religious visions. That is the country in one building: slavery and scholarship, empire and church, side by side.

And then the other thing. On the night of 23 July 1993, a group of homeless children and teenagers slept on the pavement beside this church, as hundreds of street children did then. A carload of men — several of them off-duty police — opened fire. Eight people were killed; six were minors; the youngest was eleven. Only two men were ever convicted. The wooden cross in the garden across the street carries the victims' names. It is a memorial, not an attraction, so stand quietly and read a name or two. The killings exposed how Brazil treated its poorest children, and how rarely anyone was held to account; decades on, this square is still a refuge for people with nowhere else to sleep.

The church is free and working — typically open on weekdays, roughly eight in the morning to late afternoon, closed during Mass, so verify at the door. Cover shoulders, speak softly. This stretch of the Centro is a pickpocketing hotspot: phone out of your hand, bag in front of you, and keep moving.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a working church, not a ticketed site; donations for upkeep are welcome but never required.
stops.openingHours: Working church, typically open on weekdays, roughly 08:00 to late afternoon, and closed to visitors during Mass. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: A few steps at the entrance, then a level marble floor inside. The heavy bronze doors are usually opened for you.
stops.insiderTip: The wooden cross with the victims' names stands in the garden across the street, not in front of the church. Read a name or two, quietly, and leave it as you found it.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the church, walk south down Avenida Rio Branco for about a kilometre and a half, past the CCBB cultural centre, until the grand square with the opera house opens ahead. That is Cinelândia — or take the metro one stop from Uruguaiana to Cinelândia if it is raining.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rubens Trindade, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Cinelândia: Theatro Municipal & National Library
stops.narration:
Look around and you are standing in Paris, or in a Brazilian idea of it. This square is officially Praça Floriano Peixoto, after the second president of the republic, but everyone calls it Cinelândia — 'Cinema-land' — for the movie palaces that lined it in the twentieth century. It is the showpiece of the belle époque, the 'beautiful era' of Parisian taste that swept Rio between about 1871 and 1914.

The man behind it was the mayor Francisco Pereira Passos. From 1904 he tore through the colonial city the way Baron Haussmann had torn through Paris, cutting a grand new boulevard — Avenida Central, today Avenida Rio Branco — through the old streets and lining it with monumental buildings. There is a cost to the beauty, and you should know it: to build the boulevard the city demolished most of the central cortiços, the crowded tenement houses where the poor lived, and pushed their residents up onto the hills. The favelas are part of this square's story, not separate from it.

The building in front of you is the Theatro Municipal, opened on 14 July 1909 and modelled on Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra. It sits on sixteen hundred wooden piles driven into groundwater; inside, Brazilian painters of the day — Eliseu Visconti, Rodolfo Amoedo, the Bernardelli brothers — covered the ceilings and the great curtain, the largest painting made in Brazil. Its gold leaf was restored for its centenary and it reopened in 2010, gilded again. To its left stands the National Library, the largest in Latin America, holding about nine million items; its founding collection was the Portuguese royal library, shipped over in 1810 and 1811 after the Lisbon earthquake destroyed its home. It offers guided tours on weekdays — an English tour around one in the afternoon, for a token fee — so verify the times at the door.

Stand a moment in the paradox: a colonial port that declared itself an empire, then a republic, and built an opera house and a national library to prove it belonged among the civilised nations. The square is free and open at all hours; theatre and library tours and performances cost money and run on selected days. And mind your pockets — this is the busiest pickpocketing stretch on the walk, especially along Avenida Rio Branco. The Cinelândia metro station is right here; the fare is R$7.90.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The square is free. Theatro Municipal and National Library guided visits charge a token fee — the library tour has been around R$2 — and performances are ticketed. Verify at the door.
stops.openingHours: Cinelândia square is open at all hours. Guided visits to the theatre and library run on selected weekdays; performances are usually in the evening. Check times and book ahead.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free, with kerbs at the crossings. The theatre and library interiors have stairs; lift access varies, so ask at the desk.
stops.insiderTip: Check whether the Theatro Municipal is running a guided visit that day — the foyer and the great Visconti curtain are the real show, and they are only visible on a tour or with a performance ticket.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Cinelândia walking north up Avenida Rio Branco for about eight hundred metres, then turn right into Rua Gonçalves Dias, the pedestrian shopping street. Confeitaria Colombo is at number 32, on your right, its doorway easy to miss among the shopfronts.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Confeitaria Colombo
stops.narration:
You have earned a coffee, and this is the right place to drink it. Confeitaria Colombo — 'confeitaria' means a confectioner's shop and tearoom — opened in 1894, founded by two Portuguese immigrants, Joaquim Borges de Meireles and Manuel José Lebrão. The name is a nod to the navigator; the room is a tribute to the belle époque.

Look up. Between 1912 and 1918 the halls were redone in Art Nouveau style, with huge Belgian crystal mirrors carried from Antwerp and set in carved rosewood frames, and wooden furniture carved by the artisan Antonio Borsoi. In 1922 a second floor was added with a tearoom under a stained-glass skylight, which you can glimpse through the opening in the ceiling; today the upper floor is the Cristóvão restaurant. Everything around you is over a century old and still in daily use, which is rarer than it sounds — most belle-époque interiors in Rio were demolished or gutted.

The reason Colombo matters is who sat here. In the early twentieth century this was the unofficial clubhouse of Brazilian letters and music: the composer Chiquinha Gonzaga, the poet Olavo Bilac, the politician Rui Barbosa, the writer Lima Barreto, and Heitor Villa-Lobos, whose Bachianas Brasileiras made Brazilian concert music famous abroad. People called it 'a branch of the Brazilian Academy of Letters.' Presidents and monarchs came too — Getúlio Vargas, Juscelino Kubitschek, Belgium's King Albert I and Queen Elizabeth II. A café that is also a parliament is a very Rio idea: politics and poetry settled over coffee and pastry.

Order like a local. The classic is a coffee and one of the house biscuits — the Biscoito Leque, a fan-shaped biscuit made by hand here since 1910 — or a slice from the glass case; savoury lunches and the upstairs restaurant cost considerably more than a coffee at the counter. Prices are in reais; a coffee is cheap, a full meal is a splurge, and the menu changes, so treat any figure as approximate.

It is open on weekdays and usually on Saturday, and typically closed on Sunday — verify at the door, since a landmark like this keeps its own hours. It is not a museum; it is a working café, so a purchase is expected. Step back out onto Rua Gonçalves Dias, a pedestrian shopping street, and head for the Lapa hills.
stops.entranceFeeNote: No entry fee; you pay for what you order. A coffee and a biscuit are cheap, the upstairs restaurant is a splurge — prices in reais, verify on the menu.
stops.openingHours: Typically open Monday to Saturday, from morning into the early evening; usually closed on Sunday. Confirm on the day — landmark cafés keep their own hours.
stops.accessibility: One step at the entrance, then a level ground floor. The upstairs tearoom and restaurant are reached by stairs — ask staff about lift access.
stops.insiderTip: Sit at the counter for a coffee and a Biscoito Leque, then look up at the Belgian crystal mirrors and their rosewood frames. The upstairs restaurant is lovely and much pricier.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the café, head south-west toward the Lapa hills — down Rua Gonçalves Dias, then along Rua do Riachuelo — for about a kilometre and a half. Follow the signs and the crowd up Rua Joaquim Silva; the tiled steps rise at the end of the street.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Eugenio Hansen, OFS, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Escadaria Selarón
stops.narration:
Now climb. This is the Escadaria Selarón — 'escadaria' simply means staircase — two hundred and fifteen steps rising a hundred and twenty-five metres between the Lapa and Santa Teresa neighbourhoods, and every one of them is tiled. It exists because of one obsessive man.

Jorge Selarón was a Chilean painter, born in 1947, who had lived and worked in more than fifty countries before settling in Rio in 1983. In 1990 he started repairing the broken, rubbish-strewn steps outside his own front door, covering them in fragments of tile. He began with blue, green and yellow — the colours of the Brazilian flag — and his neighbours laughed at him. He kept going for twenty-three years, and the laughter turned into the queues you see today. He called the work 'my tribute to the Brazilian people,' and insisted it was never finished: 'This crazy and unique dream will only end on the day of my death.'

Look closely at the tiles. There are more than two thousand, from over sixty countries, and most were donated by visitors who mailed or carried them here from home — you will find football crests, city names, family photographs fired into ceramic. Roughly three hundred were hand-painted by Selarón himself with the same image, over and over: a pregnant African woman. He never explained it beyond calling it 'a personal problem from my past.' He sold more than twenty-five thousand portraits of her — that is how he paid for the tiles; he was often broke, with his phone cut off and eviction notices on the door. He was found dead on his own steps in January 2013. The staircase is his grave and his monument at once.

The steps appear in Michael Jackson's 'They Don't Care About Us' video, shot by Spike Lee in 1996, and in a U2 video; they are among the most photographed places in the city. It is free and open at all hours, but come in daylight — the steps are steep, uneven and slippery when wet, and the streets just off the tourist route are quiet. Vendors at the top sell caipirinha, the cachaça-and-lime cocktail that is Brazil's national drink. If someone offers to guide you, agree a price first or decline politely. At the top, turn and look back down at the mosaic of the world.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, and open at all hours. Vendors at the top sell drinks at their own prices.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours, but visit in daylight. The steps are slippery when wet and the surrounding streets are quiet after dark.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible, honestly: 215 steep, uneven, often wet steps. The alternative is the view from the foot of the staircase.
stops.insiderTip: Hunt for a tile from your own country — there are more than two thousand from over sixty countries — and look for the hand-painted pregnant woman Selarón repeated about three hundred times.
stops.nextStopDirections: Descend the same way, then turn left along Rua Joaquim Silva to Rua dos Arcos. The arches are about five hundred metres from the foot of the steps and run away to your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Wilfredor, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Arcos da Lapa (Carioca Aqueduct)
stops.narration:
Step out of the staircase and the giant white arches run away to your right — forty-two of them in two tiers, 270 metres long and up to 17.6 metres high. This is the Arcos da Lapa, the Lapa Arches, properly the Aqueduto da Carioca, the Carioca Aqueduct. An aqueduct is a structure that carries water, and that is exactly what this was: the pipeline that kept Rio alive.

The city's first core sat among swamps, and the water was bad, so for two centuries people carried fresh water by hand from streams on the hills. Plans to bring it down from the Carioca River, on Santa Teresa hill behind you, kept failing on money and engineering until the early 1700s. A first, smaller aqueduct reached the centre in 1723; this grander replacement was built by the Portuguese military engineer José Fernandes Pinto Alpoim — the same man who designed the Paço Imperial where you started — and inaugurated in 1750. He took his inspiration from the Águas Livres Aqueduct in Lisbon. For over a century the arches fed the fountains of the city, including the one in the square where you began.

Then the water found better routes and the aqueduct was retired. In 1896 the city did something clever: it laid tram tracks along the top and turned the monument into a bridge. Ever since, the Santa Teresa tram — the bonde, affectionately the bondinho, 'little tram' — has crossed these arches to reach the hill neighbourhood above. The arches are narrow, so the tram runs on a peculiar gauge of 1,100 millimetres, an oddity engineers still enjoy. It is one of the oldest tram lines in the world, running since 1877, and Latin America's oldest electric railway. In 2011 a tram crashed here and killed six people; the line was shut for years, and the full route reopened only in 2019. A round trip on the tram costs around R$20, running roughly eight in the morning to half past six on weekdays and nine to five at weekends — verify at the station, since it changes.

The arches are free and open at all hours, and late afternoon is the best light. In front of you is Largo dos Arcos, the square where Lapa's night begins. The area is calm by day and packed after dark on weekends — fine to walk, but keep your phone in your pocket, not in your hand.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The arches are free. A round trip on the Santa Teresa tram costs around R$20 (verify at the station, and note it can be suspended for maintenance).
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours; best in late-afternoon light. Santa Teresa tram runs roughly 08:00–18:30 on weekdays and 09:00–17:00 at weekends, about every 30 minutes — confirm at the station.
stops.accessibility: The arches are viewed from a level square and street. The historic tram cars are not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Time it for late afternoon: the arches catch the low sun, and if you wait you may see the little tram cross the top. Check the tram timetable at the station before counting on a ride.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk on into Lapa, about three hundred metres south-west past the arches toward Rua do Lavradio and Avenida Mem de Sá, where the bars and music venues line the streets. That is the last stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net)., CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Lapa: Samba & the Arches
stops.narration:
You have arrived where Rio goes out. This is Lapa, the old bohemian quarter, nicknamed 'Montmartre Carioca' since the 1950s and called the cradle of Bohemian Rio — and at this hour the tables are coming out and the first chords are being tuned.

Start with the music, because it is the reason people come. Samba is the Afro-Brazilian music and dance born in Rio in the early twentieth century among the city's poor and formerly enslaved communities, and it is played here almost every night. You will also hear choro, a fast, bittersweet instrumental style older than samba; forró, a northeastern dance music; and MPB, música popular brasileira, the literate song tradition that produced names like Caetano Veloso and Chico Buarque. The venues are institutions. Beside the arches is the Circo Voador, the 'Flying Circus,' an open-air concert stage. A little further on, Fundição Progresso is a former stove factory that artists occupied in 1982 to stop it being demolished; it now holds around five thousand people for shows. Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, Bar Semente and Lapa 40 Graus fill the streets around Rua do Lavradio and Avenida Mem de Sá. And up on the main road is the Sala Cecília Meireles, one of the city's best chamber-music halls — Lapa is not only a party.

Look at the buildings, too. These are the mansions and townhouses of the nineteenth-century city, when this was a wealthy address; then the city's centre of gravity drifted south to the beaches, the national capital moved to Brasília in 1960, and the Centro — this whole district — was left to hollow out at night. Lapa's revival from the 1990s, part gentrification and part stubborn local culture, is the reason you can end a walk here with live music and a crowd.

Practicalities, honestly. Samba clubs usually charge a cover or a consumação, a minimum spend per person, so ask before you sit down and carry cash. The drink is the caipirinha — cachaça, Brazil's sugarcane spirit, muddled with lime and sugar. Lapa is busy and generally safe on the main streets after dark, but this is still central Rio: keep phones and wallets out of sight, don't wander the empty side streets late, and take a taxi or a ride-hailing car, or the metro, when you leave. The nearest metro is Cinelândia, a fifteen-minute walk back, or Glória station; the fare is R$7.90, and the metro runs until around midnight — verify the last train.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Venues usually charge a cover or a consumação — a minimum spend per person, often around R$20–R$40. Ask before you sit down and carry cash; prices vary by venue and night.
stops.openingHours: Bars and clubs open through the late afternoon and evening; live music usually starts around 21:00 and runs late. Opening days vary by venue.
stops.accessibility: Lapa's streets are flat, but the pavements are uneven and crowded at night, and most bars have a step at the door.
stops.insiderTip: Ask the door staff what is playing before you pay a cover — Lapa ranges from samba and choro to rock and electronic — and remember the venues are only minutes apart, so you can move on if one is not for you.
stops.nextStopDirections: The walk ends here, in Lapa. Wander the streets around Rua do Lavradio and Avenida Mem de Sá and pick a doorway with live music coming out of it — the bars open through the late afternoon and the music starts around nine. When you are ready to leave, walk ten to fifteen minutes back to Cinelândia metro station or take a taxi or ride-hailing car from Avenida Mem de Sá; both are safer and easier than a long walk at night. That is the tour: an empire that landed at the water, a republic that built itself an opera house, and a staircase a homesick Chilean turned into the whole world's mosaic. Obrigado — thank you for walking it.
